issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: The profile otherwise reflects fear, vigilance, avoidance of proximity/anger cues, and beliefs that others may harm her. In that context, endorsing risky or self-endangering behavior is hard to reconcile clinically, especially with no Maladaptive Strategies items or other disinhibition/externalising content to support it.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: For intimate partner physical abuse, a global appraisal that 'you can never know who will harm you' is possible but sits somewhat awkwardly beside highly specific interpersonal triggers (physical proximity, others' anger) and trauma-linked memory content. It implies diffuse unpredictability of all potential perpetrators rather than the more coherent expected pattern of threat from close others or angry interpersonal situations.

vignette:
Amahle Ndlovu is a 77-year-old African American politician who came to treatment after years of keeping her private life sealed off behind a practiced public composure. In session, she described repeated physical abuse by her husband during arguments in their home, episodes that often began with him standing too close and speaking in a tightly controlled angry voice before escalating. What remains most vivid to her is not a complete story but fragments: the heat of his body crowding her in a hallway, the look on his face when his jaw tightened, a smear of blood she saw once on her sleeve and on the bathroom sink. Those details have stayed painfully sharp while the rest feels missing, and when she edges near the memory she is flooded with guilt and cuts herself off before she can know what happened next.

In the years since, the things that pull her back are painfully ordinary. In the statehouse, if a colleague leans in to make a point or boxes her in near a doorway, Amahle feels her body tense before she can think. Even a calm expression of anger in a committee room-someone speaking through clenched restraint rather than shouting-can make her heart kick up. The sight of blood, even a minor nosebleed in a staffer or a story image on the evening news, has particular force. In those moments she becomes immediately alert and physically braced; she startles at small sounds, feels markedly less safe after dark, and checks behind her in parking garages, hallways, and outside campaign events as if someone might be coming up on her. The trigger does not stay in the present for long. It pulls up those broken pieces of the abuse, and because the recollection arrives in fragments and stops short, she is left with the same sick guilty certainty without a full account to steady herself. After one of these flashes, the rest of the day would fill with echoes of it: faces that resembled his set jaw, footsteps behind her in the corridor, the sight of a red stain on paper towels in a restroom suddenly standing out as if the memory had taught her what to keep noticing.

She has come to believe that the abuse altered her permanently. What frightens her most is not only what he did, but the conclusion she drew from surviving it: that she has changed for the worse, that normal feeling is gone for good, and that people cannot be trusted, especially when they are close enough to touch or angry enough to go cold. Holding those conclusions, she moved through ordinary encounters as if they were already suspect; a colleague stepping into her space or a restrained tone in a meeting no longer registered as neutral but as something that could turn dangerous without warning. Those beliefs now shape what she notices. She scans faces for anger, stiffens when anyone enters her physical space, and reacts to blood as if it confirms what she already "knows" about how quickly human beings can become dangerous. The same beliefs also make remembering harder. When fragments of the abuse surface, she reads her guilt as evidence that something about her is fundamentally damaged, and she pushes the memory away before it can become more complete.

That pattern has tightened over time. Because the memory is partial, she feels she has to stay on guard; if she cannot fully understand what happened, she tells herself she cannot know when it might happen again. Nights are worst. Living with that steady sense of danger became, for Amahle, its own kind of evidence; if she was still this frightened by hallways, doorways, and other people's nearness, she took it as proof that the abuse had indeed left her permanently changed and unable to trust anyone fully. She patrols the house with her attention, listening for movement, glancing over her shoulder, jolting at ordinary noises. This constant vigilance leaves her exhausted, and in that keyed-up state she is more easily snagged by proximity, anger in others, and any glimpse of blood. When she is startled or on edge, pieces of the abuse intrude more readily, but only in flashes, and the flashes deepen her conviction that she is no longer the woman she was.

The cost has become visible in her work and marriage. Amahle has begun arranging her office so no one can stand behind her, and aides have noticed that she keeps greater physical distance during meetings and abruptly ends conversations when tempers rise, even mildly. She avoids evening events when she can, knowing she feels least safe at night, and when she cannot avoid them she is preoccupied with entrances, exits, and who is walking near her. At home, her husband's proximity remains difficult to tolerate, but her mistrust has spread beyond him; she experiences wariness as a general rule about people rather than a reaction to one man. Each new episode of watchfulness or startled fear seems to her proof that the damage is lasting, and each fragment of memory that appears and vanishes strengthens her sense that something inside her is broken.

She finally sought help after a legislative meeting in which two men argued in low, controlled voices across a conference table and one leaned close to her chair. She froze, checked behind her repeatedly on the way out, and later that night could not settle, shaken by flashes of blood and by the familiar guilty feeling attached to memories she still could not fully bear to recall. She said she is afraid she will never feel normal emotions again and will spend the rest of her life braced against other people, but she is also hoping, cautiously, that if she can understand why these moments seize her so completely, she might not have to live as though danger is always just over her shoulder. Already keyed up before anything happened, she found that almost any ambiguity could harden into a warning-a figure lingering near an exit, a voice tightening across the room, even the sight of blood in an otherwise mundane setting seeming to demand immediate alarm.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not clearly show that Amahle’s negative appraisals cause or intensify the triggering stimuli themselves.
The vignette does not clearly state that intrusive trauma memories lead to reminders or cues becoming more salient or newly triggering.
The vignette shows negative appraisals contributing to threat, but does not explicitly show her sense of threat causing negative beliefs or appraisals.
The vignette shows triggers causing threat, but does not explicitly show her sense of threat generating or heightening sensitivity to triggers within the same paragraph.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not clearly show that Amahle’s negative appraisals cause or intensify the triggering stimuli themselves.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not clearly state that intrusive trauma memories lead to reminders or cues becoming more salient or newly triggering.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette shows negative appraisals contributing to threat, but does not explicitly show her sense of threat causing negative beliefs or appraisals.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Threat → Triggers: The vignette shows triggers causing threat, but does not explicitly show her sense of threat generating or heightening sensitivity to triggers within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
